# Inference on single mean

Parameter: $\mu$.

Model: $X \sim D$ with $E(X)=\mu$ and $sd(X)=\sigma$.

What the theorem provides you with the basics of this inference?
> CLT.

Gives us that: $$\overline{X} \sim N(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}})$$

The se of the distribution of $\overline{X}$ is unknown, which why we can't use the Normal dist as the sampling distribution.

The sampling distribution the t distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

100c% CI: $$\overline{x}\pm qt(c+\frac{1-c}{2}, n-1)*\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$


Hypo testing: 

$$H_0: \mu = value \quad H_{\alpha}: \mu > or < or \neq value$$
Test statistic: $$t = \frac{\overline{X}-\mu_{H_0}}{\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}$$


Null distribution: $t(n-1)$

p-val: $pt(t, n-1, lower.tail = ...)$, if it's two tailed test you would need to multiply by 2 to get the p-val.


$X= \text{Time taken by a male in the age range of 18-34 athlete to finish the Boston marathon} \sim D(\mu, \sigma)$



```{r}
library(tidyverse)
male = bm %>% filter(Year == 2010, Sex == "male", Age_Range == "18-34") %>% select(Time) 
  
summary_bm = male %>% summarize(avg = mean(Time), s = sd(Time))

pe = 207.9315
s = 40.18435	

# 95% CI
pe + c(-1, 1)*qt(0.975, 200-1)*s/(sqrt(200))

# H_0: \mu = 209 min, H_alpha: \mu \neq 209 min

t = (pe-209)/(s/(sqrt(200)))
t

pval = 2*pt(t, 200-1)
pval

#alpha = 0.05, pval = 0.25 > alpha and thus we fail to reject H_0 which is that true average time taken by a male athlete to finish the 2010 Boston marathon is 209 mins.

?t.test


```


```{r}
t.test(male, mu = 209)
```
